title: “Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me?” — the Greek has a serpent
summary: In the KJV Job asks whether he is a sea or a whale that God sets a guard over him. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, has the word δράκων, which Brenton renders “serpent”, where the KJV has “whale”.
text: KJV Job 7:12: “Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me?” Hebrew (WLC) 7:12: הֲ‍ֽיָם־אָ֭נִי אִם־תַּנִּ֑ין כִּֽי־תָשִׂ֖ים עָלַ֣י מִשְׁמָֽר. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 7:12: Πότερον θάλασσα εἰμὶ ἢ δράκων, ὅτι κατέταξας ἐπʼ ἐμὲ φυλακήν; [Am I a sea or a serpent, that you have set a guard over me?]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/7/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB07.htm.
reasoning: The question names two things, a sea and a second creature. The KJV names that creature a whale. The Greek names it a δράκων, a serpent or dragon-like creature, which Brenton prints as “serpent”. A whale and a serpent are different animals, so a reader of each text pictures a different creature beside the sea.
scope: T applies at 7:12 and only to the second creature; both texts have “sea” first. The Greek agrees with the KJV in the rest of the verse (a watch is set over him). The Hebrew is quoted so that the three texts stand together; this record does not say what the Hebrew word means, and it does not say that “whale” is outside the range of that word. The difference found is between the KJV and the Greek. The verse is Job’s speech, in verse, and the comparison is of the words printed, not of what Job meant beyond them. A record on the Greek of Job 3:8 and 41:1 and on the Hebrew word of 3:8 is published separately. This compares the wording of three texts. It does not show which wording is original. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

title: “The proud helpers do stoop under him” — the Greek has “the whales under heaven”
summary: In the KJV, if God does not withdraw his anger, the proud helpers stoop under him. In Brenton’s Greek, κήτη τὰ ὑπὸ οὐρανόν, “the whales under heaven”, are bowed under him, and the Greek has no helpers.
text: KJV Job 9:13: “If God will not withdraw his anger, the proud helpers do stoop under him.” Hebrew (WLC) 9:13: חֲח֗וּ עֹ֣זְרֵי רָֽהַב. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 9:13: Αὐτὸς γὰρ ἀπέστραπται ὀργὴν, ὑπʼ αὐτοῦ ἐκάμφθησαν κήτη τὰ ὑπʼ οὐρανόν [For he has turned away his anger; under him the sea-monsters under heaven were bowed]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/9/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB09.htm.
reasoning: The KJV has a company of helpers who are proud. The Greek has creatures of the sea and no helpers. Brenton’s own English prints “whales”. The last two of the three Hebrew words quoted stand where the KJV has “proud helpers”; the last, רָהַב, is a word the KJV prints as the name Rahab at Psalm 89:10 and Isaiah 51:9 and as “the proud” at Job 26:12.
scope: T applies at 9:13. The Greek also differs from the KJV on the first clause (the Greek has God having turned away his anger; the KJV has a condition that he will not withdraw it); the record is on the last clause. The Hebrew quoted is the end of the line, from the verb to רָהַב, with the bracketed spelling variants earlier in the verse left out. A published record, `smiteth-through-the-proud-and-crooked-serpent-or-sea-monster-and-apostate-dragon-greek`, compares the Greek at 26:12 and 26:13. That the same Hebrew word is “Rahab” in one place and “the proud” in another in the KJV is stated as a fact about the KJV’s printing; this record does not claim that “proud” is wrong at 9:13. The poem is Job’s speech. This compares the wording of three texts. It does not show which wording is original. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: “A brother to dragons, and a companion to owls” — the Greek has “sirens” and “ostriches”
summary: In the KJV Job is a brother to dragons and a companion to owls. In Brenton’s Greek he is a brother of σειρήνων, which Brenton prints “monsters”, and a companion of στρουθῶν, “ostriches”. The KJV’s own margin gives “ostriches” for “owls”.
text: KJV Job 30:29: “I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to owls.” Hebrew (WLC) 30:29: אָ֭ח הָיִ֣יתִי לְתַנִּ֑ים וְ֝רֵ֗עַ לִבְנֹ֥ות יַעֲנָֽה. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 30:29: Ἀδελφὸς γέγονα σειρήνων, ἑταῖρος δὲ στρουθῶν. [I have become a brother of sirens, and a companion of ostriches.]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/30/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB30.htm.
reasoning: The KJV names two kinds of creature that live in desolate places, dragons and owls. The Greek names sirens and ostriches. An owl and an ostrich are different birds, and the KJV’s margin at this verse offers “ostriches” for “owls”; the Greek text agrees with that margin and differs from the KJV text.
scope: T applies at 30:29, to both pairs of creatures. The KJV margin quoted is the note in the packaged KJV text (“owls: or, ostriches”); it shows that the KJV translators noted the other reading, and it is not a claim about the Hebrew. The Hebrew phrase printed after the KJV’s “companion” is בְנֹות יַעֲנָה, a word group the record does not translate or identify. The Greek word σειρήνων is a plural of an ordinary Greek word for a siren; Brenton’s English prints it as “monsters”. Neither the Hebrew word printed here nor the Greek is identified with a species. The verse is Job’s speech in verse, a comparison of his plight to the wilderness. This compares the wording of three texts. It does not show which wording is original. title: “If I covered my transgressions as Adam” — the Greek has no Adam and says “unintentionally”
summary: In the KJV Job asks whether he covered his transgressions as Adam did. Brenton’s Greek has no Adam and no comparison: Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἁμαρτὼν ἀκουσίως ἔκρυψα τὴν ἁμαρτίαν μου, “if too having sinned unintentionally, I hid my sin”. The KJV’s margin reads “after the manner of men”.
text: KJV Job 31:33: “If I covered my transgressions as Adam, by hiding mine iniquity in my bosom:” Hebrew (WLC) 31:33: אִם־כִּסִּ֣יתִי כְאָדָ֣ם פְּשָׁעָ֑י לִטְמֹ֖ון בְּחֻבִּ֣י עֲוֹֽנִי. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 31:33: Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἁμαρτὼν ἀκουσίως ἔκρυψα τὴν ἁμαρτίαν μου· [If too, having sinned unintentionally, I hid my sin;]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/31/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB31.htm.
reasoning: The KJV text names a person, Adam, as the example of someone who hid a sin. The Greek names nobody and instead describes the sin as done unintentionally. The KJV’s own margin offers “after the manner of men”, which names no person either, so the packaged KJV itself carries two readings of the Hebrew word printed here as כְאָדָם.
scope: T applies at 31:33. The Hebrew letters can be read as a proper name or as the common word for a man; this record does not say which, and does not say that the KJV’s “Adam” is wrong, only that its margin gives another reading and that the Greek has neither. Hiding sin “in my bosom” is in the KJV and has no matching phrase in the Greek line quoted (the Greek has “I hid my sin”). The verse is Job’s oath of innocence; the comparison is of the words printed. This compares the wording of three texts. It does not show which wording is original. title: “He will not afflict” — the Greek has “dost thou not think that he listens?”
summary: In the KJV Elihu ends his speech saying of the Almighty that he is excellent in power and justice and “will not afflict”. Brenton’s Greek ends the sentence with a question: ὁ τὰ δίκαια κρίνων, οὐκ οἴει ἐπακούειν αὐτόν; “as for him that judges justly, dost thou not think that he listens?”
text: KJV Job 37:23: “he will not afflict.” Hebrew (WLC) 37:23: לֹ֣א יְעַנֶּֽה. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 37:23: ὁ τὰ δίκαια κρίνων, οὐκ οἴει ἐπακούειν αὐτόν; [he who judges just things — do you not think that he gives ear?]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/37/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB37.htm.
reasoning: The KJV says the Almighty does not afflict. The Greek says that the one who judges justly listens, and puts it as a question to Job. The first is about what God does to people. The second is about whether God hears them. The final clause of the KJV is therefore a different statement from the final clause of the Greek.
scope: T applies at 37:23, to the last clause. The Hebrew two words are quoted as printed; the verb is not translated here, and this record does not say that “afflict” is outside the range of that verb. The Greek also differs earlier in the verse (“we do not find another his equal in strength”); that part is not compared here. A reader weighing God’s part in Job’s suffering sets “he will not afflict” (Elihu, KJV) beside the narrator’s words at 42:11, “all the evil that the LORD had brought upon him”; this record does not draw that comparison, and reports only that the Greek does not carry the KJV’s statement at this verse. This compares the wording of three texts. It does not show which wording is original. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: Job on the wicked: they prosper (chapter 21), and their portion is the sword and want (chapter 27)
summary: The KJV gives Job both speeches. In chapter 21 the wicked live to old age, grow mighty, and spend their days in wealth with no rod of God on their houses. In chapter 27 the wicked man’s portion with God is the sword, his children go hungry, and the rich man is gone.
text: KJV Job 21:7: “Wherefore do the wicked live, become old, yea, are mighty in power?” 21:9: “Their houses are safe from fear, neither is the rod of God upon them.” 21:13: “They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment go down to the grave.” 21:17: “How oft is the candle of the wicked put out! and how oft cometh their destruction upon them!” 27:1: “Moreover Job continued his parable, and said,” 27:13: “This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage of oppressors, which they shall receive of the Almighty.” 27:14: “If his children be multiplied, it is for the sword: and his offspring shall not be satisfied with bread.” 27:19: “The rich man shall lie down, but he shall not be gathered: he openeth his eyes, and he is not.” Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/JOB21.htm and https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/JOB27.htm.
reasoning: Both passages are given to Job by the KJV (21:1 and 27:1 each introduce him). At 21:7–13 he describes the wicked as long-lived, strong, safe and wealthy. At 27:13–19 he describes the portion of the wicked as the sword, hunger for the children, and a rich man who does not last. A reader who takes each passage as Job’s own account of how the wicked fare finds the two accounts set against each other. Chapter 21 itself already carries a qualification at 21:17, which asks how often the wicked are put out, so the same chapter holds two pictures.
scope: This sets two stretches of Job’s own speech beside each other as they stand in the KJV. It does not say that Job contradicts himself. The KJV gives no sign whether chapter 27 repeats the friends’ view in order to answer it, describes a different group of the wicked, or states Job’s considered position at a later time, and the reading of 27:13–23 is a long-standing question this record does not settle. 21:7–13 and 27:13–19 are speech in verse. Only the KJV English was compared; no Hebrew or Greek claim is made, and none is tagged. A published record, `exp-late-17-42-7`, notes that the book corrects its own speakers at 42:7.
